## Rationale

CD45RA is not a separate gene product — it is an alternatively spliced isoform of *PTPRC* (CD45). Inclusion of the variable exon 4 generates the high-molecular-weight CD45RA isoform, while skipping of exons 4–6 generates CD45RO. The RA↔RO switch is the canonical molecular correlate of the naive↔memory/activated T-cell transition: naive T cells are CD45RA-high, and TCR/CD28 activation induces a splicing program that excludes exon 4 and produces CD45RO. The key trans-acting regulator is the RNA-binding protein hnRNPLL (HNRNPLL), an activation-induced repressor that binds the exonic splicing silencer in exon 4 and promotes exon skipping; loss of hnRNPLL preserves CD45RA and impairs the RA→RO switch (Oberdoerffer et al., *Science* 2008; Topp et al., *RNA* 2008; reviewed in Lynch, *Nat Rev Immunol* 2004). Other splicing factors (hnRNP L, PTBP1, SRSF1) modulate the balance, and CD45 isoform switching is a general feature of lymphocyte activation and memory differentiation (Hermiston et al., *Annu Rev Immunol* 2003).

Cord blood mononuclear cells are a mixture in which most T cells are naive and CD45RA-high, but there is a continuum of activation/memory states, plus B cells and monocytes with distinct CD45 isoform profiles. Critically, CITE-seq measures total *PTPRC* mRNA, which is isoform-agnostic. If splicing is the dominant determinant, surface CD45RA protein should be largely decoupled from total *PTPRC* transcript abundance and instead track with the splicing program.

## Hypothesis

Cell-surface CD45RA abundance across cord blood mononuclear cells is set primarily by the activity of the *PTPRC* exon-4 splicing repressor HNRNPLL: cells with low HNRNPLL include exon 4 and display high surface CD45RA (naive state), whereas cells that have induced HNRNPLL (TCR/CD28-activated or memory-like) skip exon 4, produce CD45RO, and lose surface CD45RA. Thus HNRNPLL mRNA (negative) and CD45RO protein (negative) should be the strongest molecular correlates of CD45RA ADT, while total *PTPRC* mRNA should be a poor predictor.

## Testable predictions

1. In the CITE-seq data, within T cells and across lymphocytes, CD45RA ADT anti-correlates with HNRNPLL mRNA and with CD45RO ADT; total *PTPRC* mRNA shows only weak correlation with CD45RA ADT.
2. Isoform-resolved measurements (long-read nanopore RNA-seq or exon-4 junction qPCR) on sorted CD45RA-high vs CD45RA-low cells confirm that the exon-4 inclusion ratio, not *PTPRC* transcription rate, matches surface CD45RA.
3. CRISPRi/knockdown of HNRNPLL in cord blood T cells (or Jurkat) increases exon-4 inclusion and surface CD45RA; overexpression or anti-CD3/CD28 activation decreases CD45RA and increases CD45RO.
4. A splicing-factor score (HNRNPLL-centered) should outperform a naive/memory marker score in predicting CD45RA ADT, because it is the upstream molecular node.

## Established vs. new

The core mechanism — HNRNPLL-driven exon-4 skipping as the basis of the CD45RA→CD45RO switch — is established literature knowledge. The specific claim that this splicing program quantitatively explains cell-to-cell variation in neonatal CITE-seq surface CD45RA, and that total *PTPRC* mRNA is decoupled from surface protein, is a testable refinement/new angle in this system.
